<reason>B's honor-vs-memory distinction was established early, defended consistently, and survived the full exchange, while B's fork forced A into an increasingly strained position: A's "records vs. performs" rescue worked for passive street signs but never covered holidays, which are annually re-issued state acts ("the same authority reprints the schedule"), and A's erasure claim was blunted by B's point that archives, curricula, and sites preserve the evidence. A's strongest attack — that B's "primarily" floor is a gloss requiring endless biography trials — landed textually but was blunted by B's rejoinder that A's reading deletes the motion's only limiting word. B's closing decision rule also worked under both branches of the fossil dispute (if honor remains, stop it; if drained, continuity is no reason to keep), making B's path more robust and easier to vote on. A's clipped opening and the unaddressed holiday category were additional execution costs in an otherwise excellent performance.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's double-bind (B2.1–2.2, crystallized in B4.5): CON needs names to be live civic models to make the purge scare work and drained fossils to make removal look like amnesia — and those claims cancel. A's "past-tense record vs. present endorsement" answer (A4.1–4.2) was the debate's best counter-move, but B's "inheritance is still a choice" rejoinder re-exposed the gap for holidays and schools.</best_rebuttal>
